title: Given a `List<Employee>`, build a `Map<Long, Employee>` keyed by employee id using `Collectors.toMap`, and handle the case where two employees share the same id by supplying a merge function.
shortTitle: Collect employees into a Map<Long, Employee> keyed by id using Collectors.toMap with a merge function
keyPoints: `Collectors.toMap(keyMapper, valueMapper)` turns a stream into a Map by deriving a key and a value from each element.
When two elements produce the same key, the two-argument form throws `IllegalStateException` with a "Duplicate key" message.
The three-argument form `toMap(key, value, mergeFunction)` resolves collisions by passing the existing and new value to a `BinaryOperator`.
The merge function returns the value to keep: `(existing, replacement) -> existing` keeps the first, `(a, b) -> b` keeps the last.
For employees keyed by id, the merge function lets you pick the more complete or more recent record instead of crashing.
`toMap` makes no ordering or null guarantees; a null value from the value mapper also throws `NullPointerException`.

s1_definition.oneliner: `Collectors.toMap(Employee::getId, e -> e)` builds a `Map<Long, Employee>`, and the third argument, a merge function, decides which employee survives when two share the same id.
s1_definition.profdef:
`Collectors.toMap` is a collector that reduces a stream into a `Map`.

- **Key mapper** – a `Function` that extracts the map key from each element, such as `Employee::getId`.
- **Value mapper** – a `Function` that extracts the map value, such as `Function.identity()` to store the employee itself.
- **Merge function** – a `BinaryOperator` called only when two elements map to the same key; it receives both values and returns the one to keep.
- **Map supplier** – an optional fourth argument that chooses the concrete `Map` type, such as `LinkedHashMap::new`.

Without a merge function, a duplicate key is treated as a programming error and `toMap` throws immediately.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, Rajesh is handed a stack of employee records and told to file one folder per employee id. The id is the label on the folder (the key mapper) and the record is what goes inside (the value mapper). If two records carry the same id, Rajesh cannot put both in one folder, so he follows a written rule: keep the record with the most recent join date. That written rule is the merge function. Without it, Rajesh would freeze and refuse to file anything, which is exactly what `IllegalStateException` does.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  List<Employee>  (two records share id 101)
        │
        │  stream().collect(toMap(getId, identity, merge))
        ▼
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │           Collectors.toMap                   │
  │                                              │
  │  for each Employee e:                        │
  │    key   = keyMapper(e)     e.getId()        │
  │    value = valueMapper(e)   e                │
  │                                              │
  │    key already present?                      │
  │        │ no               │ yes              │
  │        ▼                  ▼                  │
  │   put(key,value)   merge(existing, value)    │
  │                         │                    │
  │                         ▼                    │
  │                 keep the returned value      │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        │
        ▼
  Map<Long, Employee>
```

```text
  Duplicate key 101
        │
        ├── two-arg toMap ──▶ IllegalStateException ("Duplicate key 101")
        │
        └── three-arg toMap ──▶ merge(existing, replacement)
                                   │
                   ┌───────────────┼────────────────┐
                   ▼               ▼                 ▼
            (e,r) -> e       (e,r) -> r     (a,b) -> later joinDate
            keep first       keep last       keep most recent
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
When Priya asks for a `Map<Long, Employee>` so HR can look up any employee by id, `Collectors.toMap` is the direct tool. You hand it two functions: `Employee::getId` to produce the key and `Function.identity()` to store the employee as the value. For clean data where every id is unique, that two-argument form is all you need.

The moment two employees share an id, the two-argument form stops and throws `IllegalStateException` with a "Duplicate key" message. This is not a flaw; it is the collector refusing to silently discard data. It is the same instinct Rajesh had when he was told to file two records under one folder label and could not decide which one to keep.

The fix is the three-argument overload, which adds a merge function. That function runs only on a collision and receives the value already stored and the value from the new element. Whatever you return is the value that survives. `(existing, replacement) -> existing` keeps the first record seen, `(a, b) -> b` keeps the last, and a rule like comparing join dates keeps the most recent and meaningful record.

Two traps remain. The value mapper and the merge function must never return null, because `toMap` is built on `Map.merge`, which rejects nulls with a `NullPointerException`. And the default result is an unordered `HashMap`, so reach for the four-argument overload with `LinkedHashMap::new` or `TreeMap::new` when order matters, and wrap with `collectingAndThen` plus `unmodifiableMap` when the lookup should stay read-only.

In our banking work the lesson is simple: decide your collision policy before you collect, write it as the merge function, and let the stream enforce it for you.

Remember one sentence: `toMap` without a merge function crashes on duplicate keys, so supply a merge function to choose which value wins.
